rv.q: Those names – along with Constance Wu, Tramell Tillman and Michael Oberholtzer – can't help but raise expectations that, frustratingly, go largely unmet.
While Shit. Meet. Fan. isn’t all that persuasive, it delivers jolts of spiky humor and a cast of hardworking household names.
The pacing of the show, and its staging are both arresting and off-putting.
The latest theatrical proof of this tenet comes courtesy of Shit. , playwright Robert O’Hara’s 105-minute send-up of moneyed white privilege, toxic bro-havior, and the illusion of privacy.
Not funny enough for straight-up comedy, populated with characters too thin for drama, and lacking a wicked sense of caricature, it struggles to find a consistent, coherent voice.
What might have been a searing examination of privilege and hypocrisy instead feels like an exhausting exercise in endurance.

rv.q: Those intentions are clear but he does not successfully skewer his subjects. Maybe there is a light roasting but the satire mostly misses the mark.
The actors work together seamlessly to make some fundamentally unlikable characters entertaining enough to tolerate for a few hours, waiting for their well-deserved uppance to come.
While Shit. Meet. Fan. doesn't always spark; it's the kind of theater we want to see more of.

cn.t: O'Hara's star-studded satire on privilege and toxic masculinity provokes laughs and gasps but ultimately frustrates, with critics finding the premise contrived and characters too despicable to care about despite committed performances.
